summary: Some networks, such as financial data networks, treat latency as important as other metrics when choosing paths. This standards-track RFC extends IS-IS Traffic Engineering with performance metrics like delay so that path selection can use them. It was replaced by RFC 8570.

eli5.summary: Sometimes the fastest route matters more than the shortest one. This lets routers advertise how long each link takes so others can pick the quickest path.

questions: how does is-is advertise performance metrics
what are is-is te metric extensions
how can i use latency in routing decisions
subtitle: Adding performance metrics like latency to IS-IS routing decisions.

tldr.problem: Networks that need to choose paths based on latency and other performance metrics have no standard way to distribute this information through IS-IS routing.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7810 defines new sub-TLVs that carry performance metrics such as delay, delay variation, packet loss, residual bandwidth, available bandwidth, and utilized bandwidth in IS-IS advertisements.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now use performance information to select paths based on criteria like low latency, which is critical in financial and other latency-sensitive networks. RFC 8570 later updated and expanded these metrics.

today: RFC 7810 is a Proposed Standard and was obsoleted by RFC 8570, which provides updated and expanded performance metrics for IS-IS.

sections.title: Adding Performance to Routing Decisions
sections.content:
IS-IS is a routing protocol that routers use to tell each other about available paths. Traditionally, IS-IS made routing decisions based on hop count or cost metrics, not on how fast data actually travels. In networks where latency matters greatly -- such as financial data networks where traders compete on microseconds -- a longer path with lower latency is better than a short path with high delay. RFC 7810 extends IS-IS Traffic Engineering (RFC 5305) to distribute network-performance information so that routers can make path-selection decisions based on metrics like latency, rather than just cost.

The RFC defines which performance metrics can be advertised and how routers should handle them. It does not specify how routers should measure performance; that is left to other standards like RFC 6374 (measuring delay in MPLS networks).
sections.eli5: This document lets routers share how fast or slow their links are. Routers can then pick the quickest path, not just the shortest one.

sections.title: Performance Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
IS-IS advertisements are made up of pieces called TLVs (Type-Length-Value). RFC 7810 adds seven new sub-TLVs that sit inside existing IS-IS Extended Reachability TLVs:

  • Unidirectional Link Delay (Type 33): The average latency on a link in microseconds, encoded as a 24-bit integer. Maximum value 16.777215 seconds.
  • Min/Max Unidirectional Link Delay (Type 34): Minimum and maximum measured delay values, each 24-bit integers in microseconds.
  • Unidirectional Delay Variation (Type 35): The variation (jitter) in link delay, 24 bits in microseconds.
  • Unidirectional Link Loss (Type 36): Packet loss as a percentage of sent traffic, using a 24-bit field where the basic unit is 0.000003%.
  • Unidirectional Residual Bandwidth (Type 37): Available link capacity minus reserved RSVP-TE bandwidth, encoded as IEEE floating-point in bytes per second.
  • Unidirectional Available Bandwidth (Type 38): Residual bandwidth minus measured non-RSVP-TE traffic, as IEEE floating-point bytes per second.
  • Unidirectional Utilized Bandwidth (Type 39): Measured bandwidth actually in use, encoded as IEEE floating-point bytes per second.

Delay and delay-variation values are integers in microseconds. Bandwidth values are floating-point in bytes per second. All values (except residual bandwidth) MUST be rolling averages over a configurable period.
sections.eli5: Each link can report seven different numbers about itself: how long it takes to send data, how much it varies, how many packets get lost, and how much bandwidth it has free or in use.

sections.title: Anomalous Bit and Thresholds
sections.content:
Some sub-TLVs include an Anomalous (A) bit. When an operator sets a maximum threshold for a metric, the A bit is set to 1 if the measured value exceeds that threshold, and cleared when the value falls below a configured reuse threshold. When the A bit is clear, the sub-TLV represents steady-state performance and can be used for initial path computation. When the A bit is set, a router can use the metric to decide whether to fail traffic to a backup path or compute an entirely new path.

The RFC requires implementations to support configurable accelerated advertisement thresholds. If a metric falls outside a configured bound (or exceeds a threshold), the router should advertise the change immediately rather than waiting for the next regular update interval. To prevent network instability, only one threshold (high or low) may be used per metric.

The default measurement interval SHOULD be 30 seconds, and the default announcement periodicity SHOULD be 120 seconds. Implementations MAY suppress re-advertisements of small changes that fall within configured thresholds.
sections.eli5: Routers can raise a warning flag when a link starts performing badly. Other routers see the flag and decide whether to use that link, or find a better path instead.

sections.title: Integration with IS-IS TE
sections.content:
The performance sub-TLVs defined in RFC 7810 are carried in the IS-IS Extended Reachability TLV (TLV 22, defined in RFC 5305), the Inter-AS Reachability Information TLV (TLV 141), and the Multi-Topology IS-IS TLV (TLV 222). They may be used with or without the TE subsystem. However, if these sub-TLVs are present, then Interface Address or Neighbor Address sub-TLVs (IPv4 or IPv6) MUST also be present, so that the information can be properly associated with a link.

The data distributed by IS-IS TE Metric Extensions can be used for many purposes: to enhance Constrained-SPF (CSPF) path computation in label switched path setup, to provide data for ALTO servers (RFC 7285) that advertise network topology and cost, or to support Weighted ECMP (equal-cost multipath) that balances traffic across multiple equal-cost paths while weighing their performance characteristics.
sections.eli5: These new metrics fit into the existing IS-IS structure and can be used to set up tunnels, balance traffic, and help tools understand which paths are fastest.

sections.title: Security and Stability
sections.content:
Performance metrics like latency and bandwidth can be sensitive information that operators may not want to disclose. RFC 5304 describes how to authenticate IS-IS Link State PDUs with cryptographic signatures, which can prevent a man-in-the-middle attacker from delaying real-time data by falsifying performance metrics.

In large networks, if measurement intervals are set too low, the flood of re-advertisements could overwhelm routers. The RFC recommends a default measurement interval of 30 seconds and a default announcement periodicity of 120 seconds. The minimum announcement periodicity is 1 per second. Implementations should allow suppression of re-advertisements when values change by small amounts. These controls help ensure that networks remain stable and that the routing protocol does not become a source of instability.

RFC 7810 does not specify how to measure performance, but implementers are cautioned that delay measurements SHOULD NOT include significant buffer delay or queuing delay; these should be avoided by measuring with a traffic class that experiences minimal queuing or by summing delays of component links.
sections.eli5: Network operators need to keep these metrics private, and routers need to avoid talking too much, or the network gets overwhelmed. Routers should measure real delay, not the delay from waiting in a queue.
